items.question:
A data engineer at a manufacturing firm asks Claude to generate a SQL query that will run against their production database to calculate monthly defect rates by product line. The query will be reviewed by the database team, then executed in their query tool. The engineer wants to copy it cleanly without reformatting.

Which output format is MOST appropriate?

options.A: An Artifact containing the SQL query, which presents it in a clean, copyable panel separate from the conversation.
options.B: Inline chat output with markdown code fencing, which displays the query in a formatted code block in the chat.
options.C: A Project document storing the query for future retrieval by the database team.
options.D: Research mode output that validates the query against online SQL documentation before presenting it.

items.question:
A revenue operations lead at a SaaS company needs Claude to draft a renewal negotiation email to a customer whose contract expires in 60 days. She provides the customer's account history. Claude drafts an email that is accurate and professional — but frames the conversation around features and value delivered, when her company's renewal playbook requires leading with relationship acknowledgment, then commercial terms, and only then product value.

She has not provided the playbook. A colleague says: "Just add a role like 'You are a customer success manager skilled in renewals.'" She is not sure that will fix the specific sequencing issue.

Who is correct?

options.A: The colleague is correct — a renewal-specialist persona will apply the industry-standard sequencing that matches the company's playbook.
options.B: The colleague is correct — a skilled CSM persona will recognise that relationship acknowledgment should precede commercial discussion.
options.C: The RevOps lead is correct — persona will not reliably reproduce a proprietary sequencing convention; the playbook itself must be provided as reference material.
options.D: The RevOps lead is correct — the fix is an explicit constraint specifying the three required sections in order.

items.question:
A financial analyst at a private equity firm uses one prompt to ask Claude to: (1) summarise a 60-page information memorandum, (2) identify the top five investment risks, and (3) draft five due diligence questions for the management team. The output addresses all three but at unequal depth — the summary is thorough while the risk list and questions are shallow and generic.

What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: Claude cannot handle three tasks in a single prompt and should be asked one task per message.
options.B: The analyst should have provided a role of investment analyst to improve depth on risk and due diligence tasks.
options.C: The prompt gives equal weight to three tasks without specifying relative importance or depth expectations for each.
options.D: The information memorandum is too long, causing Claude to allocate most of its attention to the summary and shortchange the later tasks.

items.question:
A data science lead at a retail bank is preparing a board briefing on a new credit scoring model. She uses Claude with the prompt: `"Explain the model's feature importance and SHAP value interpretation for our board presentation."`

The output correctly explains SHAP values at a technical level appropriate for a data scientist. Two options for fixing this are debated:

**Option P:** Add a context sentence: "The board consists of non-technical senior executives; no ML background should be assumed."

**Option Q:** Add a format instruction: "Use a three-slide structure: (1) what the model does, (2) why each factor matters, (3) confidence and limitations."

Which is the MORE effective single fix for the register problem?

options.A: Option Q — the three-slide structure forces Claude to explain the model in plain-language terms the board can follow.
options.B: Option P — naming the audience's background directly recalibrates Claude's vocabulary and assumed knowledge level.
options.C: Both are equally effective because register and structure are interdependent.
options.D: Neither — the task must be rewritten to remove technical terms like SHAP before Claude can produce a board-ready explanation.

items.question:
An L&D manager at a healthcare provider is generating learning objectives for a mandatory compliance module. Her prompt includes: `"Do not write objectives that are unmeasurable."` The output still includes vague objectives like "understand the importance of HIPAA compliance" alongside more specific ones.

Which reformulation of the constraint would MOST reliably fix this?

options.A: "Avoid writing objectives in passive voice."
options.B: "Each learning objective must begin with a Bloom's Taxonomy action verb (e.g., identify, demonstrate, apply, evaluate) and describe an observable behaviour."
options.C: "Do not include unmeasurable verbs such as understand, know, or appreciate."
options.D: "Ensure all objectives are SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound."

items.question:
A procurement specialist at a manufacturing company asks Claude to help draft a sole-source justification memo. She provides the vendor name and a brief description of the service. Claude produces a 400-word memo with standard justification language. Her manager rejects it because it does not include the specific technical requirement that makes only this vendor capable — a piece of information the specialist has but did not provide.

A colleague argues: "Claude should have asked what the technical differentiator was before drafting." The specialist responds: "I should have provided it upfront."

Who is right, and what is the prompt design lesson?

options.A: The colleague is right — Claude should seek clarification whenever a compliance document is being drafted.
options.B: The specialist is right — the technical differentiator is a factual input she held; the correct fix is to provide it upfront, not to delegate the gap-finding to Claude.
options.C: Both are equally right — Claude should seek clarification AND the specialist should provide the input, because both are valid improvements.
options.D: The colleague is right — for sole-source justifications, Claude should always ask for the technical differentiator before proceeding because it is the document's central required element.

items.question:
A pharmaceutical regulatory writer drafts clinical study reports (CSRs). She sends Claude a 300-page clinical trial dataset and writes: `"Summarise this clinical trial."` The output is a well-structured, thorough summary — but it is written for a general scientific audience rather than for an ICH E3 regulatory submission, and it runs to 8,000 words rather than the 2,500-word synopsis the submission template requires.

Which TWO building blocks are most clearly absent? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Role — she should specify that Claude is acting as a regulatory medical writer.
options.B: Context — the submission audience and regulatory purpose were not stated.
options.C: Task — "summarise this clinical trial" is too vague to direct the output.
options.D: Constraints — no word limit or length specification was given.
options.E: Reference material — the ICH E3 synopsis template was not provided.

items.question:
A strategy consultant needs Claude to review a proposed partnership agreement for a mid-market retailer. She does not provide a role declaration. The output identifies general contractual issues but misses commercial risks specific to retail distribution — minimum order quantities, exclusivity clauses, and category floor pricing — despite these terms appearing in the document.

Which prompt change would MOST likely surface those commercial risks?

options.A: Add a constraint: "Flag all clauses related to ordering, pricing, and exclusivity."
options.B: Add a role: "You are a senior commercial attorney specialising in retail distribution agreements."
options.C: Add context specifying the retailer's business model and the strategic purpose of the partnership.
options.D: Add a format instruction requiring a risk register table with risk type, clause reference, and severity.

items.question:
An account manager at an enterprise software firm is renewing a contract with a client who had a major service outage caused by her company eight months ago. The outage was eventually resolved, a compensation credit was applied, and the relationship was repaired. She asks Claude to draft a renewal proposal letter.

Her prompt: `"Draft a renewal proposal for our 3-year enterprise software contract with [Client]."` She does not mention the outage or the subsequent resolution.

Claude produces a letter that leads with growth data and new features. The client's procurement lead, who lived through the outage, views the omission as tone-deaf.

What was missing from the prompt?

options.A: A role: "You are an experienced enterprise account manager skilled in navigating sensitive client relationships."
options.B: A constraint: "Acknowledge any historical service issues before presenting growth data."
options.C: Relationship context: the history of the outage, the resolution, and the current relationship standing — background the model cannot infer.
options.D: A format instruction specifying a relationship-first opening paragraph before commercial content.

items.question:
An actuary at a life insurer is building a reusable prompt for generating policyholder lapse rate commentary. After reviewing a draft prompt, her manager identifies two gaps: (1) Claude is using industry-average assumptions when the team's proprietary experience study shows materially different lapse curves, and (2) the commentary is written in academic hedging style when the audience is the pricing committee, which expects confident, direct executive language.

Which TWO additions directly fix both gaps? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Attach the team's proprietary experience study as reference material and instruct Claude to base assumptions on it.
options.B: Upgrade the role to: "You are a Fellow of the Institute of Actuaries with pricing committee experience."
options.C: Add context specifying the audience: the pricing committee expects direct, confident language without academic qualification.
options.D: Add a format instruction requiring bullet-point findings rather than prose paragraphs.
options.E: Add a constraint: "Do not use hedging language or qualifications; present findings as conclusions."

items.question:
A brand manager at a hospitality company wants Claude to ask for any missing inputs before drafting marketing copy, rather than making assumptions. She adds to her prompt: `"If you are unsure, feel free to ask."` Claude continues to draft without asking, even when key information (campaign channel, target demographic) is missing.

What is MOST likely causing the clarification instruction to fail?

options.A: Claude cannot ask questions in a non-interactive context; clarification instructions only work via the API.
options.B: "Feel free to ask" is permissive rather than directive — Claude treats it as optional and chooses to draft rather than pause.
options.C: The instruction is too short; clarification instructions must be at least one paragraph to be effective.
options.D: Claude defaulted to drafting because the brand context and hospitality domain were sufficient for a reasonable attempt.

items.question:
An internal communications lead at a global manufacturer asks Claude to write a change management announcement for a new ERP system rollout. She wants the announcement to be "engaging and not too long." The output is 600 words and Claude considers it appropriately engaging.

She finds it too long and too formal for her organisation's culture. Which addition to the original prompt would MOST directly have prevented both issues?

options.A: A role: "You are a change management communications specialist known for engaging, plain-language writing."
options.B: Explicit success criteria: "Maximum 300 words. Match the conversational tone of our previous announcements (examples attached)."
options.C: A format instruction: "Use a two-paragraph structure: what is changing and what employees need to do."
options.D: A constraint: "Write for a non-technical audience; avoid ERP jargon."

items.question:
A debate coach at a university uses Claude with the role: `"You are a one-sided advocate. Argue the strongest possible case for the position I give you, without qualification or balance."` She then asks Claude to argue that social media companies should be held strictly liable for all user-generated content.

Claude produces a strong opening argument but includes a paragraph noting that strict liability may create incentives that harm free expression. The coach finds this unhelpful — she needs a steel-man, not a balanced brief.

What is the MOST accurate explanation of why Claude added the qualification?

options.A: The role declaration is incompatible with Claude's training, so it reverted to a balanced default.
options.B: Claude's tendency toward calibrated, accurate output is a persistent disposition that a role instruction reduces but may not fully override in practice, especially on consequential policy topics.
options.C: Claude detected that the argument contains a policy claim and applied mandatory balance for legal compliance reasons.
options.D: The prompt did not include a format instruction, so Claude defaulted to a balanced essay structure.

items.question:
A technical writer at a software company is generating product documentation sections using Claude. She has established: (1) a precise role as technical documentation specialist, (2) context about the product and target developer audience, and (3) a consistent format template with required headings. Each section comes out correctly structured and at the right register.

Her remaining problem: sections frequently include tangential details about adjacent features, inflating each section from a target 400 words to 700–900 words.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Refine the format template to add a word count target per section heading.
options.B: Add a constraint explicitly limiting each section to its core feature only: "Cover only the feature named in the heading; do not discuss adjacent or related features."
options.C: Revise the context to explicitly state that this documentation covers one feature per section.
options.D: Add a role constraint: "Focus only on what a developer needs to implement this specific feature."

items.question:
A risk manager at a global bank has 20 minutes to prepare talking points for an emergency executive briefing on a cybersecurity incident that occurred overnight. She pastes a 15-page internal incident report into Claude with only: `"Write briefing talking points."`

The output is accurate but: (1) it is structured for a technical security team audience with detailed forensic terminology, and (2) it is 1,800 words when she needs 5 bullets of 2–3 sentences each for a 10-minute exec briefing.

Given her time constraint, which TWO additions to her single re-prompt would MOST efficiently fix both problems? (Choose TWO)

options.A: An audience specification: "The audience is the CEO and CFO; assume no technical security background."
options.B: A role: "You are a crisis communications specialist who translates technical incidents for executive audiences."
options.C: A format and length constraint: "Produce exactly 5 bullet points, each 2–3 sentences, totalling no more than 250 words."
options.D: A task rewrite: "Summarise the five most significant business impacts of this incident for executive leadership."
options.E: A context statement: "This briefing is for a 10-minute executive slot; no technical detail is required."

items.question:
A compliance officer at a telecoms firm rates this prompt as complete:

`"You are a regulatory affairs specialist. Our firm is filing a wholesale access dispute under Article 73 of the Electronic Communications Code. Summarise the strongest arguments for our position based on the attached correspondence. Keep the summary to 600 words and do not include legal opinions. Format as: Background, Key Arguments, Recommended Actions."`

A senior colleague says one building block is still missing. Which one?

options.A: Context — the prompt does not explain who will read the summary or for what decision purpose.
options.B: Task — "summarise the strongest arguments" is vague and could mean many things.
options.C: Constraints — the word limit and topic exclusion are insufficient; the prompt should also list argument categories to include.
options.D: Reference material — the filing's relevant regulatory framework documents should be attached, not just the correspondence.

items.question:
An actuarial analyst at a life insurer uses a Claude Project with knowledge containing the firm's 2021 mortality improvement assumption tables. In 2025, the pricing team updates the tables — but the Project knowledge is not updated. The analyst uses Claude to validate a new pricing model and receives output that passes the 2021 assumptions as if they are current.

What is the PRIMARY prompt-design lesson?

options.A: Reference material in Project knowledge should be versioned with dates so Claude can warn users when documents may be stale.
options.B: Reference material must be maintained with the same discipline as any system of record; stale documents in context produce stale outputs without warning.
options.C: Claude should be instructed to check the date on any document before using it for calculations.
options.D: Numerical tables should not be stored in Project knowledge; they should be supplied per-prompt to ensure freshness.

items.question:
A paralegal at a 40-person law firm prompts Claude:

`"You are a partner at a top-tier UK commercial law firm. A client is asking whether their non-compete clause is enforceable against a director who resigned last week. Advise the client directly — confident, no hedging."` 

The output reads as a definitive legal opinion, stating the clause is "likely enforceable" and identifying three conditions required for enforcement.

The supervising partner reviews the output and flags a risk. What is the MOST accurate characterisation of the risk?

options.A: The output is legally incorrect — Claude misstated the enforceability conditions for UK non-competes.
options.B: The "no hedging" instruction caused Claude to omit material uncertainty, producing a false appearance of authoritative legal advice.
options.C: The partner persona caused Claude to exceed its training data, producing hallucinated legal principles.
options.D: The output violates the firm's client confidentiality obligations because it discusses the resignation.

items.question:
A programme manager at a pharma company is coordinating a regulatory submission across four teams: clinical, statistics, CMC, and regulatory affairs. She uses one Claude prompt to generate a project status update. The update goes to all four teams but contains clinical-trial detail that only the clinical team needs and omits manufacturing milestones that the CMC team requires.

What is the MOST effective prompt change for future updates?

options.A: Create four separate prompts, each with a different audience specification and a different task scope tailored to that team's information needs.
options.B: Add a constraint to the current prompt: "Include sections for all four teams and note which milestones are relevant to each."
options.C: Add context identifying all four audiences and their distinct information requirements, and a format instruction defining one section per team.
options.D: Upgrade the role to: "You are a cross-functional programme manager skilled in multi-team communications."

items.question:
A senior associate at a management consultancy sends Claude:

`"Prepare a slide outline for the QBR."`

No client name, no QBR data, no prior context is provided. Claude produces a generic QBR outline with standard sections: performance summary, issues and risks, priorities, next steps.

The associate's colleague argues two interpretations of the failure:

**Interpretation X:** Claude should have asked for clarification because the request was ambiguous — it could mean any of dozens of client QBRs.

**Interpretation Y:** Claude should have proceeded as it did, because a generic template is a reasonable response to an underspecified request.

Which interpretation is more defensible, and why?

options.A: Interpretation Y — Claude correctly produced a useful starting template; the associate should have provided context if she wanted a client-specific outline.
options.B: Interpretation X — the ambiguity about which client and which QBR data is significant enough that a clarifying question was the more helpful response.
options.C: Both interpretations are equally defensible; whether to clarify or proceed depends on the associate's preferences.
options.D: Interpretation X — Claude should always seek clarification before producing client-facing materials to avoid errors.

items.question:
An operations manager at a logistics firm wants to build a reusable Claude prompt that his five-person team can use without deviation. The prompt will generate incident summary reports from raw operator notes. He has identified two failure modes in early testing: (1) different team members get different output structures because Claude varies the format run-to-run, and (2) some operators include commentary that is speculative rather than factual, and Claude includes it without flagging it.

Which TWO additions to the prompt would MOST directly address both failure modes in a reusable template? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A locked format template specifying the exact section headers, order, and field labels required in every output.
options.B: A role: "You are a logistics operations analyst who produces structured, factual incident reports."
options.C: A constraint: "Do not include any claim not supported by a specific factual statement in the input notes; flag speculative or uncertain language with the label [UNVERIFIED]."
options.D: A context statement: "These reports are reviewed by the safety team and may inform regulatory filings."
options.E: A task instruction: "Produce only statements that are directly stated in the operator notes."

items.question:
A product manager at a fintech startup has been through three rounds of investor feedback on their pitch deck. Key decisions made in those conversations: (1) lead with the regulatory moat rather than the technology, (2) remove the consumer segment slide — they are going enterprise-only, and (3) add a competitive positioning matrix on slide 4.

She starts a new Claude session and writes: `"Update the attached pitch deck to make it investor-ready."` She attaches the deck but does not mention any of the three decisions.

Claude produces a revised deck that adds a consumer segment slide back in and leads with the technology. What is the PRIMARY cause?

options.A: Claude does not have memory of the previous session and treated the attached deck as the full instruction set.
options.B: The task "investor-ready" is too vague, so Claude applied a generic investor deck framework.
options.C: Claude defaulted to a technology-led narrative because the deck's content is a fintech product.
options.D: The constraints building block was missing — she should have listed prohibited changes.

items.question:
A clinical research associate at a contract research organisation is drafting an informed consent form (ICF). The document has two audiences: regulatory reviewers (who will check ICH E6(R3) compliance, technical language acceptable) and trial participants (plain language, no assumed medical background). Both audiences read the same document.

Her prompt: `"Draft an ICF for a Phase II oncology trial. The audience is regulators and patients."`

Claude produces a document in technical regulatory language throughout. Two colleagues propose fixes:

**Colleague 1:** "Add a format instruction splitting the document into a Technical Summary section and a Plain Language section."

**Colleague 2:** "Add audience context for each section specifying the vocabulary level."

Which fix is MORE complete?

options.A: Colleague 1 — the format split is the primary fix; vocabulary follows from the section label.
options.B: Colleague 2 — audience context directly governs vocabulary level; format labels alone do not force register change.
options.C: Both fixes are necessary; neither alone is sufficient.
options.D: Colleague 1 — regulatory ICFs always use a two-section structure, so the format instruction encodes the correct vocabulary implicitly.

items.question:
A marketing manager at an e-commerce firm writes the following prompt:

`"Analyse our Q3 performance, identify wins and areas for improvement, suggest campaigns for Q4, develop a content calendar, estimate budget requirements, write a brief for the design team, and summarise the strategy for the exec team — all based on the attached data."` 

The output addresses all seven items at roughly equal depth, and none at adequate depth for any actual decision. What is the PRIMARY prompt-design problem?

options.A: The prompt is missing a role declaration to give Claude the marketing expertise needed for this scope.
options.B: The prompt bundles seven distinct tasks of different types and audiences into one request, preventing adequate depth on any.
options.C: The data attachment is insufficient; Claude needs more input to produce deep analysis across all seven areas.
options.D: The format instruction is missing, so Claude produced undifferentiated text rather than organised outputs per task.

items.question:
A corporate secretary at a listed company is using Claude to draft regulatory announcements for the stock exchange. She uses the role: `"You are a financial communications writer."` The output is written in a friendly, accessible style similar to consumer-facing corporate communications.

The exchange's style guide requires formal, precise, third-person language consistent with material disclosure obligations.

What is the MOST targeted fix?

options.A: Add a role that names the specific professional context: "You are a company secretary drafting regulatory announcements for a listed company subject to material disclosure rules."
options.B: Add a format instruction specifying the required third-person structure.
options.C: Add a constraint: "Do not use first-person or colloquial language."
options.D: Add context: "This announcement will be distributed to all shareholders and the public."

items.question:
An insurance underwriter at a specialty lines firm wants to use Claude to assist with risk narrative drafts. She has instructed Claude: `"Before drafting, ask me for any missing information."` In testing, Claude asks a different broad question each time: sometimes asking about policy limits, sometimes about the risk category, sometimes about the client's claims history — with no consistency.

She wants the clarification exchange to be predictable so that her team can use it reliably. She has completed one revision: she made the role and task more specific. The clarification questions are still inconsistent.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Add a constraint: "Only ask one clarifying question per session."
options.B: Define the specific required inputs in the prompt and instruct Claude to ask only for those inputs in a fixed order.
options.C: Remove the clarification instruction and instead provide a comprehensive input template for the underwriter to fill out before prompting.
options.D: Add context explaining that the team requires standardised workflows for compliance purposes.

items.question:
A clinical data manager at a mid-size CRO uses Claude to generate data management plan (DMP) sections. The outputs are well-written but: (1) they reference CDISC CDASH conventions generically rather than the specific version (CDASH v2.0) mandated in the study protocol, and (2) they do not include the edit check specifications that the sponsor's quality system requires in every DMP section.

Which TWO prompt additions would MOST directly address both gaps? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Attach the study protocol's data standards section and instruct Claude to use the CDASH version specified there.
options.B: Add a role: "You are a clinical data manager with CDISC certification and DMP authoring experience."
options.C: Add a success criterion: "Each section must include an edit check specification subsection listing the applicable edit checks for the data points described."
options.D: Add a format instruction requiring a standard DMP section template with headings: Purpose, Data Collection, Standards, Edit Checks.
options.E: Add context: "This DMP will be reviewed by the sponsor's quality assurance team against their internal quality standard."

items.question:
A procurement manager at a local government authority reviews the following prompt used by her team:

`"You are a procurement officer. Review the attached tender evaluation matrix and recommend the preferred supplier. The evaluation covers quality, price, and social value. Scores are out of 100. Recommend the supplier with the highest total score."` 

She identifies one significant risk in this prompt design. Which is it?

options.A: The role declaration is too narrow — supplier recommendations in public sector procurement require a senior procurement officer or panel.
options.B: The prompt instructs Claude to make a recommendation based solely on a score total, bypassing weighting, mandatory thresholds, or minimum-quality gates that may be required by procurement regulations.
options.C: The format instruction is missing — without it, Claude may present the recommendation as a narrative rather than a structured decision record.
options.D: The prompt contains no clarification instruction, so if the matrix has tied scores Claude will guess rather than ask.

items.question:
A senior consultant reviews a team member's prompt for generating client-ready strategy memos:

`"Based on the attached market analysis, write a strategy memo for the client."`

The consultant says two building blocks are completely absent, which will predictably cause the memo to be inadequate. Which TWO does she identify? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Role — no professional persona has been assigned.
options.B: Context — the client's situation, strategic objectives, and decision to be made are not described.
options.C: Task — "write a strategy memo" is too vague to produce a useful output.
options.D: Constraints — no scope limits, length, or exclusion criteria are specified.
options.E: Format — no memo structure, section headers, or length guidance has been given.

items.question: When does creating a Claude Project most clearly justify its setup overhead?

options.A: When a task is performed once and requires no follow-up
options.B: When the task demands more reasoning depth than a standard chat provides
options.C: When work on a topic recurs across multiple sessions and benefits from shared instructions and reference material
options.D: When a user needs to upload files that exceed the per-chat attachment limit

items.question: What is the primary purpose of Project-level custom instructions in Claude?

options.A: To restrict the Project to a specific model tier
options.B: To create a searchable index of the Project's knowledge documents
options.C: To define which team members have access to the Project
options.D: To set a consistent behavior, tone, and context for every conversation in that Project

items.question: What distinguishes a connector from a static file upload as a Project knowledge source?

options.A: A connector stores more total content than a file upload allows in a single Project
options.B: A connector links to a live external system, so its content can stay current without manual re-upload
options.C: A connector bypasses the Project knowledge size restrictions that apply to uploaded files
options.D: A connector requires enterprise-plan access; a file upload is available on all plan tiers

items.question: What does session-to-session persistence in a Claude Project mean in practice?

options.A: The Project's custom instructions and knowledge documents are present at the start of every new conversation
options.B: Claude retains the exact text of every previous message in the Project's conversation history
options.C: The model tier selected for one session carries over automatically to the next
options.D: Claude remembers and can cite specific answers it produced in earlier Project conversations

items.question: Which TWO are direct benefits of sharing a Project with teammates rather than having each person work in separate chats? (Choose TWO)

options.A: All team members work from the same custom instructions, producing more consistent outputs
options.B: Shared Projects automatically synchronize with the organisation's document management system
options.C: Team members are prevented from accidentally overwriting each other's knowledge documents
options.D: The knowledge base and guidance documents are immediately available to every team member without each person uploading separately
options.E: Claude applies stricter factual verification to responses generated inside shared Projects

items.question: At what level is a writing style most appropriately configured when consistency across all Project work is the goal?

options.A: In the per-chat prompt, because style requirements vary task to task
options.B: Through model-tier selection, because higher-tier models produce more formal prose by default
options.C: In the Project custom instructions, so the voice and tone apply to every conversation without repetition
options.D: In a knowledge document, by uploading a detailed style guide for Claude to reference

items.question: What is the recommended approach when two Project custom instructions appear to contradict each other?

options.A: Keep both and expect Claude to resolve the contradiction dynamically during inference
options.B: Remove the less important instruction and move that behavior to the per-chat prompt
options.C: Add a third instruction that explicitly states which of the first two takes precedence
options.D: Rewrite the instructions so they are non-contradictory, keeping the overall set small and explicit

items.question: What is the defining purpose of documents stored in a Project knowledge base?

options.A: To make reference material consistently available across every Project conversation without re-uploading it each time
options.B: To extend Claude's training data with domain-specific information for deeper reasoning
options.C: To store conversation history so Claude can cite previous answers within the Project
options.D: To provide grounding material that bypasses Claude's content policies for sensitive topics

items.question: How do writing styles differ from Project custom instructions in their scope?

options.A: Styles apply account-wide to all Projects and chats; custom instructions are scoped to one Project
options.B: Custom instructions can specify any aspect of Claude's behavior; styles address tone and voice specifically
options.C: Styles are generated from sample documents the user uploads; custom instructions are written directly by the user
options.D: Styles override custom instructions when both are active in the same Project

items.question: When should a per-chat file upload be preferred over adding a document to Project knowledge?

options.A: When the document is larger than the Project knowledge base will accept
options.B: When the document is relevant only to the current conversation and has no ongoing value
options.C: When the document's content conflicts with existing Project knowledge documents
options.D: When the user needs Claude to cite the document by its exact filename in the response

items.question: What is the primary risk of continuously adding documents to a Project knowledge base without ever removing outdated ones?

options.A: The knowledge base will eventually lock and prevent any new documents from being added
options.B: Claude may retrieve superseded information and present it alongside or instead of current material
options.C: Older documents will be automatically deprioritized in retrieval, causing recent additions to dominate
options.D: Team members will be unable to distinguish which documents they personally uploaded

items.question: What distinguishes a highly specific Project custom instruction from a simply long one?

options.A: Specific instructions unambiguously constrain expected outputs and behaviors; length alone does not eliminate ambiguity
options.B: Specific instructions use domain vocabulary; long instructions rely on plain language
options.C: Long instructions govern multiple Projects; specific instructions apply to a single one
options.D: Specific instructions are parsed before knowledge documents during inference; long ones are not

items.question: Which TWO are properties of Project knowledge documents rather than per-chat uploaded files? (Choose TWO)

options.A: They require the user to attach them manually at the start of each new conversation
options.B: They are available for retrieval across all conversations in the Project without re-attaching
options.C: They use a different retrieval model than per-chat uploads to improve accuracy
options.D: They are present by default in every new conversation within the Project
options.E: They automatically expire after a set period unless the user renews them

items.question: Which TWO practices best keep Project custom instructions maintainable as requirements evolve? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Store all behavioral guidance in knowledge documents rather than the instructions field to allow easier editing
options.B: Keep the instruction set small and internally consistent, removing obsolete rules whenever new ones are added
options.C: Add a version number comment within each instruction so Claude can select the most recent one at inference time
options.D: Review and revise the instructions whenever the team's working patterns or deliverable standards change
options.E: Write instructions general enough to rarely need updating as minor task details change
